source.title: Simply B1 Preliminary for Schools: 8 Complete Practice Tests (2019, revised exam from 2020)
source.answerKeyOrigin: Prepared for WordHop from the supplied reading text; not a publisher-provided answer key.
source.explanationOrigin: Written for WordHop with evidence from the supplied text.

questions.explanation: Don's mother wants him to pass a message to his father, who should call the garage. Don is not being asked to make that call himself.
questions.evidence: Can you tell your dad to phone the garage for me?

questions.explanation: Payment is required by the end of each month. Paying by the twenty-fifth earns a discount but is not the final deadline.
questions.evidence: All student accommodation must be paid by the last day of the month.

questions.explanation: On Wednesdays the coffee shop closes at 1 pm, so it cannot serve coffee late that afternoon. Late Saturday opening happens only every third Saturday.
questions.evidence: Wednesday half day until 1.00pm.

questions.explanation: Tim cannot keep the Friday dinner arrangement and proposes Saturday or the following weekend instead. He is changing the date, not the activity.
questions.evidence: I can't make it for dinner on Friday, so, can we arrange Saturday?

questions.explanation: The advertised membership discounts are available this week. The gym is open all day, but classes have separate hours and Saturday morning is reserved for children.
questions.evidence: Great discounts on membership this week

questions.explanation: Medicine and the modern world covers new technologies such as printing body parts and future treatments. These are useful developments aimed at healthier lives.
questions.evidence: they are already used to print body parts and may one day print human hearts

questions.explanation: The space-food talk is unusual and interactive: visitors taste food and can try making it. Tanya can participate rather than only listen.
questions.evidence: You can even try making space food, yourself!

questions.explanation: Science in our world is explicitly for all ages and includes making a kite to take home. This gives Sally and her young sister a suitable creative activity together.
questions.evidence: In this family-friendly talk for all ages

questions.explanation: Understanding the weather compares the latest forecasting technologies with older ones and displays historical equipment. It connects outdoor weather interests with technological development.
questions.evidence: describe how these have developed from past technologies

questions.explanation: Comedy and Science uses humour to explain the history of scientific discoveries and includes a fun quiz. This fits Neil's wish for an enjoyable, accessible talk.
questions.evidence: Learn how scientists first discovered medicines and technologies in very unusual ways.

questions.explanation: C appears intended, but the source wording is not precise. The passage describes a 1.5-degree goal that is not being met; it does not say that an earlier scientific prediction was wrong. A, B and D also misrepresent the passage. This question is not included in the score.
questions.evidence: The goal was to stop the world's temperature from rising more than 1.5 degrees Celsius.
questions.reviewNote: The passage gives a target, not an original prediction. C appears intended but is not fully supported by the wording. This question is excluded from the score.

questions.explanation: Greta refused to attend school in order to draw attention to climate change. Her example then inspired students elsewhere.
questions.evidence: who refused to go to school to draw attention to climate change

questions.explanation: Liz presents the students' reaction as necessary after governments have done very little. The statement 'It had to happen' supports A rather than criticism of the young people.
questions.evidence: It had to happen.

questions.explanation: The passage describes more serious future consequences if effective action is not taken, including floods, destructive storms and rising sea levels.
questions.evidence: Rivers would flood, storms would destroy towns and cities by the sea.

questions.explanation: Young people are taking the lead because governments have not acted sufficiently. C captures the movement's purpose without claiming everyone has stopped work or permanently left education.
questions.evidence: the younger generation ... have decided to take the lead

questions.explanation: G refers back to the mother's joke about how much time the writer spent on the computer and admits that it was true.
questions.evidence: My mum used to joke that I spent more time on the computer than speaking to her!

questions.explanation: F explains why the parents initially supported computer use. The next sentence gives examples of computers being necessary at school and work.
questions.evidence: You use them at school for projects and at work when you're an adult.

questions.explanation: A introduces a new, more serious stage after excessive gaming and missed lessons. The following paragraph describes the resulting health problems.
questions.evidence: My health began to suffer.

questions.explanation: H connects the lack of exercise to illness. The next sentence illustrates that illness through frequent colds and generally feeling unwell.
questions.evidence: Because I was indoors all day, I wasn't exercising.

questions.explanation: D marks the change from being upset to understanding the parents' point. It leads into listening to them and reducing time on the computer.
questions.evidence: I listened to them and slowly began to spend less time on my computer.

questions.explanation: 'Influence' means an effect on the style or development of something. Edinburgh's comparison with Athens is explained through its architecture, not its climate.
questions.evidence: buildings ... inspired by classical architecture

questions.explanation: Buildings can be 'inspired by' a style, meaning their designers took ideas from it. 'Built by classical architecture' would not be grammatical or logical.
questions.evidence: many important buildings, (22) ... by classical architecture

questions.explanation: 'Popular with' is the correct expression for being liked by a group of people. Here that group is the city's many tourists.
questions.evidence: very (23) ... with the hundreds of thousands of tourists

questions.explanation: A 'tourist attraction' is a place that visitors want to see. The sentence contrasts today's busy visitor destination with the historical city.
questions.evidence: the busy tourist (24) ... of today

questions.explanation: 'Amount' is used with the uncountable noun 'waste'. 'Number' would require a plural countable noun.
questions.evidence: the (25) ... of waste from the human population

questions.explanation: A festival is an event, so 'events' fits the example of the Fringe Festival. The other nouns do not name this kind of organised occasion as naturally.
questions.evidence: the Fringe Festival which takes place every summer

questions.explanation: The whole clause 'That Speakers' Corner exists at all' acts as a singular subject. It needs 'is' before the complement 'a puzzle'.
questions.evidence: That Speakers' Corner exists at all (27) ... a puzzle to foreigners.

questions.explanation: 'Where' introduces a relative clause describing what can happen in the place just mentioned, Hyde Park's Speakers' Corner.
questions.evidence: a place in Hyde Park, London, (28) ... anyone can say anything

questions.explanation: 'Since then' connects the beginning of the tradition with the present perfect 'have spoken', referring to the period from that time until now.
questions.evidence: Many famous people have spoken at Speakers' Corner (29) ... then.

questions.explanation: 'More ... than ...' contrasts the audience's two possible motives: entertainment rather than interest in the speakers' views.
questions.evidence: more for entertainment (30) ... because they are interested

questions.explanation: 'What they have to say' means the things they want to say. This noun clause is the object of the preposition 'in'.
questions.evidence: interested in (31) ... they have to say

questions.explanation: 'Other countries' means countries beyond the UK. 'Different' also fits before the plural noun with the same general meaning.
questions.evidence: over the UK and even in (32) ... countries
